paragraphs: A regression model can predict a range of possible numerical outcomes rather than a single value. For these predictions to support decisions, their stated uncertainty needs to agree with what actually happens. This paper examines that agreement, called probabilistic calibration, in neural network regression, an area less studied than calibration in classification.

The authors conduct a large empirical comparison of methods that improve calibration through recalibration, conformal prediction, or regularization. These approaches adjust predictions or influence training in different ways. They also introduce differentiable recalibration and regularization methods, allowing calibration-related adjustments to participate in gradient-based optimization.

The findings distinguish calibration from sharpness: predictions should reflect uncertainty accurately while remaining informative. Regularization offers a favorable balance between these aims, whereas post-hoc methods achieve better probabilistic calibration in the study. The authors attribute this advantage to conformal prediction’s finite-sample coverage guarantee and show that quantile recalibration is a special case of conformal prediction. A shared, reproducible implementation supports fair comparisons between the methods.
icml-2023-a-large-scale-study-of-probabi.tldr: A large regression study compares calibration methods and connects quantile recalibration to conformal prediction.

paragraphs: Learning a decision tree involves choosing a sequence of splits, and finding the best tree within a depth bound can require substantial computation. This paper introduces Blossom, an algorithm designed to provide useful trees quickly while continuing to search for better ones when more computation is available.

Blossom adapts a leading dynamic programming approach into an anytime algorithm. The significance of this design is that practical use does not depend on waiting until an optimality proof is complete. The algorithm can produce a candidate tree along the way, while retaining the ability to establish optimality through further search.

In experiments, Blossom learns trees comparable to those produced by standard heuristics with virtually no computational overhead. Additional computation can substantially improve accuracy, including for deep trees that existing exact methods struggle to handle. On most datasets, its ability to prove optimality is comparable to the best exact methods. These results suggest a useful connection between fast heuristic-style results and the more demanding search for an optimal bounded-depth tree.
icml-2023-blossom-an-anytime-algorithm-f.tldr: Blossom quickly produces competitive decision trees and can improve them toward bounded-depth optimality with additional computation.

paragraphs: When a model encounters a changed data distribution, its accuracy may change even if no labels are available to measure it. This paper studies how to estimate accuracy from the predictions themselves. It argues that individual prediction confidence provides only part of the useful information.

The additional signal is dispersity: how predictions spread across categories over a collection of examples. The authors’ central insight is that strong performance should be associated with both confident individual predictions and dispersed overall predictions. They use the nuclear norm of the prediction matrix to capture these two properties together, and also investigate alternative measurements such as mutual information maximization.

Experiments cover multiple model architectures, datasets, and distribution shifts. The nuclear norm gives more accurate and robust accuracy estimates than existing methods in these evaluations. The authors also examine its limitations and an improved variant for severe class imbalance. That qualification matters because the distribution of predicted categories is part of the estimator’s signal, and the paper explicitly studies how an uneven class distribution affects its use.
icml-2023-confidence-and-dispersity-spea.tldr: Combining prediction confidence with category dispersity improves label-free accuracy estimation under distribution shifts in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Many systems evolve continuously through space and time, while transformers represent their inputs through discrete observations. This creates a mismatch: a model built around sampled points does not automatically guarantee that its output behaves continuously between them. The paper addresses this issue with the Continuous Spatiotemporal Transformer, or CST.

CST is designed specifically for continuous dynamical systems. Its central mechanism is optimization in Sobolev space, which provides the framework’s guarantee of continuous, smooth output. Smoothness is therefore a property addressed by the model’s mathematical formulation, rather than something inferred solely from how its predictions look at the observed samples.

The authors compare CST with traditional transformers and other methods for modeling dynamics across space and time. They report superior performance on several tasks involving both synthetic and real systems, including learning brain dynamics from calcium imaging. The contribution combines a structural guarantee about output behavior with empirical evidence of predictive usefulness. The smoothness guarantee concerns continuity of the modeled output; the reported performance advantages are findings from the evaluated tasks.
icml-2023-continuous-spatiotemporal-tran.tldr: CST uses Sobolev-space optimization to guarantee smooth, continuous outputs and improves performance on several spatiotemporal modeling tasks.

paragraphs: A layer’s Lipschitz constant describes how strongly changes in its input can affect its output. Controlling this sensitivity is relevant to neural network training stability, generalization, and robustness. This paper focuses on estimating a related quantity for convolutional layers: their spectral norm.

The authors introduce an upper bound that is precise, fast to compute, and differentiable. Their method combines circulant matrix theory with Gram iteration, a new alternative to power iteration. Gram iteration has superlinear convergence, making its convergence behavior a central part of the proposed computational advantage. Differentiability also makes the bound useful within an optimization procedure, beyond evaluating an already trained layer.

Experiments compare the approach with other leading methods and report advantages in precision, computational cost, and scalability. The authors then apply it to Lipschitz regularization of convolutional neural networks, obtaining competitive results against concurrent approaches. These findings connect the estimation method to a concrete training use: efficiently computing a usable sensitivity bound can help make sensitivity control practical during neural network optimization.
icml-2023-efficient-bound-of-lipschitz-c.tldr: Gram iteration provides a fast, differentiable spectral-norm upper bound that supports practical Lipschitz regularization of convolutional networks.

paragraphs: Two neural networks can be compared by averaging how much their outputs differ across a training set. This function space distance describes differences in behavior, but computing it from the data can require retaining or repeatedly processing many examples. The paper seeks a compact substitute for those repeated comparisons.

The proposed Linearized Activation Function TRick, or LAFTR, approximates a ReLU network as a linear network with stochastic gates. This representation leads to an efficient approximation of function space distance using only one additional parameter per network unit. The compact summary is intended to preserve information useful for later calculations without repeatedly traversing the full training set.

The method outperforms other parametric approximations that require more memory. In continual learning, it is competitive with leading nonparametric approximations that store many training examples. The authors also demonstrate accurate influence-function estimation and detection of mislabeled examples without expensive full-dataset iterations. Together, these results show several uses for a small stored approximation of how a network behaves on its training data.
icml-2023-efficient-parametric-approxima.tldr: LAFTR compactly approximates differences between ReLU networks’ outputs, supporting continual learning and data analysis without repeated full-dataset processing.

paragraphs: Matching systems assign people to opportunities, such as students to schools or applicants to interviews. Such decisions need to account for individual preferences and relevant merit, which may mean fit, need, or future performance. The difficulty is that merit inferred from observable information remains uncertain, including when machine learning supplies the estimates.

This paper formalizes individual fairness for two-sided marketplaces while explicitly respecting that uncertainty. Its formulation treats uncertainty as both a possible source of unfairness and something that can help address it. The authors then develop a linear programming framework for finding distributions over allocations that maximize utility subject to their fairness requirements.

Working with distributions means the framework chooses how allocations should be randomized, rather than only selecting one fixed assignment. The authors also show robustness to perturbations in the estimated parameters of merit distributions. This property matters when the framework uses machine learning estimates: the proposed optimization accounts for uncertainty, and its robustness result addresses sensitivity to errors in the parameters used to describe that uncertainty.
icml-2023-fairness-in-matching-under-unc.tldr: The paper formalizes fairness under uncertain merit and optimizes randomized allocations with robustness to perturbations in estimated distribution parameters.

paragraphs: Correlation clustering groups vertices using information about which pairs should belong together. This paper studies its Min Max objective and develops fast algorithms for complete graphs. The goal is to obtain clusterings with a formal quality guarantee while reducing the computational burden that prevents existing approaches from handling larger networks.

The central construction is a new semi-metric called the correlation metric. It assigns pairwise information that guides the clustering algorithms toward deciding whether two vertices should share a cluster. The authors use this construction to obtain constant-factor approximation guarantees and describe their methods as the first purely combinatorial approximation algorithms for this problem.

The empirical results show a favorable tradeoff: relative to prior work, the algorithms give up little objective quality while achieving substantially shorter running times. They also handle larger networks that known algorithms find effectively intractable. The theoretical guarantee is stated for complete graphs, while the experiments establish the practical speed and quality tradeoff. Together, these contributions make approximate solutions more accessible at network sizes that were previously difficult to process.
icml-2023-fast-combinatorial-algorithms-.tldr: A new correlation metric enables fast combinatorial constant-factor approximations for Min Max correlation clustering on complete graphs.

paragraphs: A model’s confidence can be misleading when it is overconfident about incorrect predictions. This paper explores an additional reliability signal: whether the model’s internal representation agrees with that of a foundation model. The aim is to improve judgments about when a prediction is likely to be trustworthy.

Directly comparing internal representations is difficult because their coordinate systems may be arbitrarily rotated or have different numbers of dimensions. The authors address this mismatch through neighborhood agreement. Instead of relying on matching coordinates, their measure compares neighborhood structure across the two latent spaces, providing a way to assess agreement despite incompatible representations.

The measured agreement is strongly correlated with prediction reliability in the reported findings. Combining it with the model’s existing confidence after training significantly improves reliability. The paper supports the approach with theoretical analysis and extensive failure-detection experiments across multiple datasets, including both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings. The practical contribution is an additional post-hoc signal for recognizing unreliable predictions, based on agreement between representations rather than confidence alone.
icml-2023-great-models-think-alike-impro.tldr: Agreement between a model’s latent neighborhoods and a foundation model’s improves post-hoc reliability estimates and failure detection.

paragraphs: Compressing a neural network saves memory, but the way compressed parameters are accessed also affects execution speed. This paper introduces ROAST hashing, a model-agnostic compression method that explicitly accounts for hardware memory access. It targets the costs of both training and deploying large models.

ROAST uses a lightweight mapping to group parameters so they share stored values. Its mapping aligns memory access with the order in which operations need parameters, making use of cache hierarchies. The method also introduces global weight sharing, which the authors support theoretically and empirically as superior to the local sharing used by HashedNet.

Compared with HashedNet, the reported speedups reach approximately 25 times for training and 50 times for inference. On text and image classification tasks, ROAST enables training and deployment with memory footprints approximately 10 to 100 times smaller. These are reported results rather than fixed speedups for every workload. The broader contribution is to connect parameter sharing with efficient hardware access, so reducing stored weights can also translate into practical computational benefits.
icml-2023-hardware-aware-compression-wit.tldr: ROAST combines global parameter sharing with cache-aware access to reduce model memory and accelerate execution relative to HashedNet.

paragraphs: An image counterfactual asks how an observed image would change under a different causal circumstance. Answering this requires more than producing a plausible image: the change must follow the relationships represented by the causal model. This paper develops a general generative framework for estimating such counterfactuals with deep structural causal models.

The authors combine ideas from causal mediation analysis with advances in generative modeling. Their new causal mechanisms handle structured, high-dimensional variables such as images. Mediation gives the framework a way to distinguish direct effects from effects transmitted indirectly through other variables, alongside the total effect of a change.

The experiments demonstrate accurate abduction and estimation of direct, indirect, and total effects. Here, abduction is the inference step needed to connect an observed case with the model’s counterfactual reasoning. The authors assess these capabilities through the axiomatic soundness of the resulting counterfactuals. The stated contribution therefore joins high-fidelity image generation with a causal evaluation criterion, examining whether generated alternatives behave consistently with the counterfactual properties being tested.
icml-2023-high-fidelity-image-counterfac.tldr: New deep causal mechanisms support high-fidelity image counterfactuals and accurate effect estimation under axiomatic counterfactual evaluation.

paragraphs: Noisy-OR Bayesian networks model dependencies in binary data, including relationships involving hidden variables. Learning complex hidden structures has largely relied on variational inference. This paper identifies problems with existing approaches: some cannot represent explaining-away, while mean-field approaches can become trapped in poor local optima and require slow sequential parameter updates.

The authors propose parallel max-product inference as an alternative and derive a fast stochastic training procedure that scales to large datasets. The approach directly addresses the computational bottleneck of sequential updates while providing a different way to learn networks with complex latent structure.

On large, sparse real datasets, the method improves test performance over a prior approach for hierarchical noisy-OR networks. It also recovers more ground-truth parameters from cluttered synthetic scenes. For a two-dimensional blind deconvolution problem and related variants, including binary matrix factorization, it succeeds where the evaluated variational approach fails severely and is up to two orders of magnitude slower. These findings support the alternative across several distinct learning and reconstruction settings.
icml-2023-learning-noisy-or-bayesian-net.tldr: Parallel max-product learning improves noisy-OR network results and speed over evaluated variational approaches on several benchmarks.

paragraphs: Gradient descent can be highly sensitive to its learning rate. For convex Lipschitz functions, choosing a rate with optimal convergence requires information about the distance from the starting point to the solution set. This paper introduces D-Adaptation to achieve the desired asymptotic rate without knowing that distance in advance.

The method uses a single optimization loop without backtracking or line searches. Its theoretical result reaches the optimal convergence rate for this function class without the extra multiplicative logarithmic factors present in earlier parameter-free methods. It also requires no additional function-value or gradient evaluations at each step, making the adaptation computationally practical.

The authors test SGD and Adam variants on more than a dozen machine learning problems, including large-scale vision and language tasks. In these experiments, the method automatically matches hand-tuned learning rates. The theory and experiments establish different parts of the case: the convergence guarantee concerns convex Lipschitz optimization, while the broader machine learning evaluations demonstrate the practical behavior of the proposed variants.
icml-2023-learning-rate-free-learning-by.tldr: D-Adaptation removes learning-rate tuning while achieving an optimal asymptotic convex convergence rate and matching hand-tuned rates in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks approximate solutions to partial differential equations, but they can converge to incorrect, trivial solutions. This paper examines how the points sampled during training contribute to such failures. The authors hypothesize that successful learning depends on propagating solution information from initial or boundary conditions into the interior of the domain.

They show that poor sampling can accompany propagation failures characterized by strongly imbalanced equation residuals, which measure how much the predicted solution violates the equation. Their Retain-Resample-Release algorithm, or R3, incrementally accumulates collocation points in regions with high residuals. This directs training attention toward regions where satisfying the equation remains difficult, with little or no computational overhead.

The paper also extends R3 to respect causality in time-dependent equations. The authors theoretically analyze its behavior and compare its effectiveness and efficiency with baselines across several PDE problems. The contribution links a proposed explanation of training failure to an actionable sampling strategy, with both analysis and empirical evidence supporting the strategy’s ability to mitigate those failures.
icml-2023-mitigating-propagation-failure.tldr: R3 sampling concentrates training points in high-residual regions to mitigate propagation failures in physics-informed neural networks.

paragraphs: An advertiser buying impressions across multiple channels wants to maximize total conversions while meeting an overall budget and return-on-investment constraint. Individual auctions are handled by the channels, so the advertiser cannot directly optimize every purchase. Instead, the available controls are each channel’s budget and target return on investment.

The paper analyzes how much these two controls can accomplish. Under the studied formulation, optimizing only channel-level ROI targets can produce conversions arbitrarily worse than the global optimum. By contrast, optimizing only channel budgets can achieve the globally optimal conversion total. This identifies budget allocation as a sufficient control for reaching that optimum in the analyzed problem.

The authors then consider learning with bandit feedback, reflecting limited knowledge of auctions and how channels procure impressions. They provide an efficient algorithm that learns per-channel budgets whose resulting conversions approximate the global optimum. The distinction between the results matters: budget control can attain optimality in the optimization analysis, while the learning algorithm provides an approximation under limited feedback.
icml-2023-multi-channel-autobidding-with.tldr: Per-channel budgets can achieve the studied global advertising optimum, and a bandit algorithm learns budgets that approximate it.

paragraphs: A randomized ensemble selects one classifier at inference time rather than running every ensemble member. This makes it attractive when computation is limited and adversarial robustness is important. However, earlier constructions were found more vulnerable than initially claimed, raising questions about when random selection actually provides a useful defense.

This paper develops theoretical results on the limits of randomized ensemble classifiers, including necessary and sufficient conditions for their usefulness. Those results provide a foundation for deciding when the approach has value, instead of treating randomization itself as evidence of robustness. The authors use this understanding to design BARRE, a boosting algorithm for training robust randomized ensembles.

Experiments demonstrate BARRE’s effectiveness against strong adversaries whose perturbations are bounded in the infinity norm, across several architectures and datasets. The contribution therefore combines a characterization of what randomized ensembles can achieve with a training method informed by that characterization. Its empirical defense results concern the tested attack setting, while the theoretical analysis addresses the broader conditions and limits of usefulness.
icml-2023-on-the-robustness-of-randomize.tldr: The paper characterizes randomized ensembles’ robustness limits and introduces BARRE, a training method effective against tested infinity-norm-bounded attacks.

paragraphs: Learning a directed acyclic graph requires optimizing a score while avoiding directed cycles. NOTEARS-style formulations express the cycle restriction through a continuous, non-convex constraint, creating difficult optimization problems. This paper studies their optimality challenges and introduces an algorithm organized around the ordering of graph nodes.

The method has two levels. The outer level searches over topological orders by swapping pairs of nodes, using a specially designed procedure to generate promising candidate swaps. Given an order, the inner level uses existing solvers that handle linear constraints. This separates the search over node arrangements from optimization under a chosen arrangement.

The authors guarantee convergence to a local minimum or a KKT point under weaker conditions than previous work. These are local optimality or constrained stationarity outcomes, rather than a claim of global optimality. Extensive experiments show better objective scores than leading alternatives. The algorithm also works as a post-processing step that can significantly improve solutions produced by other methods, making the ordering-based search useful beyond training a graph model from scratch.
icml-2023-optimizing-notears-objectives-.tldr: Topological node swaps improve NOTEARS-style objective scores while providing local-minimum or KKT guarantees under weaker conditions than prior work.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented language models can answer knowledge-intensive questions using retrieved passages, but encoding many passages is expensive. Precomputing their representations reduces this cost, yet loses quality because those stored representations do not depend on the current question. This paper introduces LUMEN to combine reusable representations with question-specific processing.

LUMEN precomputes most of the retrieval representation, then completes the encoding when a question arrives. The live encoder is conditioned on that question and fine-tuned for the task. This divides the computation between work that can be reused and work that adapts the retrieved information to the particular input.

Across multiple question-answering tasks, LUMEN significantly outperforms pure precomputed memory while costing much less than Fusion-in-Decoder. The authors also report better performance than either approach at matched compute budgets, with its advantage over Fusion-in-Decoder increasing as model size grows. These findings support retaining a live encoding stage: some question-conditioned computation can recover useful quality while most representation work remains reusable, improving the measured balance between answer quality and computational cost.
icml-2023-pre-computed-memory-or-on-the-.tldr: LUMEN combines precomputed passage representations with question-conditioned encoding to improve the measured quality–compute tradeoff in retrieval-augmented question answering.

paragraphs: The maximum-flow problem asks how much flow a network can carry under its constraints. Ford-Fulkerson is a widely used algorithm for computing that quantity. This paper explores whether learned predictions can make it faster by supplying a useful starting flow before the algorithm performs its remaining work.

The approach seeds Ford-Fulkerson with predicted flows. Its motivation is that a prediction may capture part of the structure of a good solution, giving the algorithm a more useful starting point. The authors provide theoretical performance results expressed in terms of prediction quality, connecting the computational benefit to how informative the supplied prediction is.

The paper also evaluates the method on image segmentation, a computer vision application of network flows. Strong empirical results complement the theoretical analysis in that setting. The contribution is a way to incorporate predictions into an established combinatorial algorithm, with an explicit analysis of prediction quality and an application demonstrating practical value. The stated theory makes prediction quality part of the performance story rather than assuming every prediction is equally helpful.
icml-2023-predictive-flows-for-faster-fo.tldr: Seeding Ford-Fulkerson with predicted flows yields prediction-quality-dependent performance guarantees and strong image-segmentation results.

paragraphs: Scaling transformers has produced major advances in language modeling, motivating the question of how far similar scaling can go in vision. This paper presents ViT-22B, a vision transformer with 22 billion parameters, together with a recipe for training it efficiently and stably at that size.

The authors evaluate the resulting model across a wide range of downstream tasks. In many evaluations, they keep its learned features fixed and train only a lightweight linear model. Improvements in that setting show the usefulness of the representations produced by the large model, without requiring the entire network to be retrained for each evaluation.

The experiments show performance increasing with scale and report several additional benefits: a better fairness–performance tradeoff, improved robustness, and leading alignment with human visual perception as measured through shape-versus-texture bias. These observations broaden the case for scaling beyond task performance alone. The paper presents the results as evidence of the potential for language-model-like scaling in vision and as practical progress toward making that scale achievable.
icml-2023-scaling-vision-transformers-to.tldr: ViT-22B demonstrates stable, efficient vision-transformer scaling with reported gains in downstream performance, robustness, and other model properties.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks offer energy and efficiency benefits when implemented in hardware, but their training is difficult. Their activations are non-differentiable, and outputs accumulate over time. Surrogate gradients make backpropagation possible, yet introduce approximation errors that can grow as they pass backward through multiple layers.

The paper proposes surrogate module learning to reduce this accumulated gradient error. Surrogate modules create shortcut paths that send more accurate gradient information to selected parts of the spiking network. A new loss jointly trains the main network and improves the modules’ ability to serve as useful surrogates.

The authors demonstrate that gradient error drops substantially when the surrogate modules’ outputs are close to the spiking network’s output. That condition links module quality to the intended training benefit. Experiments report consistent, significant performance improvements across all evaluated datasets, including CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, and ES-ImageNet. For a spiking ResNet-34 on ImageNet, the abstract reports an accuracy increase of 3.46%. The findings support shortcut gradient pathways as a way to improve direct spiking-network training.
icml-2023-surrogate-module-learning-redu.tldr: Surrogate modules provide shortcut gradient paths that reduce training error when their outputs closely match the spiking network’s output.

paragraphs: A model’s storage cost depends on both its parameter count and the number of bits used for each parameter. Consequently, a larger model stored at lower precision can occupy the same space as a smaller model stored at higher precision. This paper asks which combination gives the best zero-shot performance for a total bit budget.

The authors develop inference scaling laws using more than 35,000 experiments. They study models from 19 million to 176 billion parameters across BLOOM, OPT, NeoX/Pythia, and GPT-2, with 16-bit inputs and parameter precision ranging from 3 to 8 bits. This setup compares compression choices together with model scale.

The findings identify 4-bit precision as almost universally optimal for the measured balance between total model bits and zero-shot accuracy. Improvements to that tradeoff were difficult to obtain; the reported successful choices involved smaller independently quantized parameter blocks and the quantization data type. The result supports 4-bit parameters for the studied objective while retaining the qualification that the finding is almost universal, rather than an exception-free rule.
icml-2023-the-case-for-4-bit-precision-k.tldr: Across extensive experiments, 4-bit parameters are almost universally optimal for balancing total model bits against zero-shot accuracy.

paragraphs: Persistent homology describes topological features of data and tracks how they change across scales. The persistent Laplacian combines this multiscale perspective with a higher-order extension of the graph Laplacian. It contains information about homology together with additional geometry that homology alone does not capture.

This paper investigates whether that richer description is useful as an embedding: a representation supplied to downstream classification or regression methods. The authors also extend the persistent Laplacian to cubical complexes, enabling its use with images. This makes the theoretical construction applicable to a data format important for practical learning tasks.

Evaluations on MNIST and MoleculeNet show the persistent Laplacian consistently outperforming persistent homology across the tested tasks. The findings support the usefulness of representations that retain geometric information alongside topology. The paper’s contribution is both methodological and empirical: it expands the construction to images and provides the first investigation of its effectiveness for downstream prediction, connecting a mathematical development to measured classification and regression performance.
icml-2023-the-persistent-laplacian-for-d.tldr: Persistent Laplacian embeddings combine topology with additional geometry and outperform persistent homology on the evaluated MNIST and MoleculeNet tasks.

paragraphs: Adding data from a different distribution can help a target task, but the benefit need not grow with the amount added. This paper proves that generalization error can first improve with a small amount of out-of-distribution data, then become worse than if none had been included.

The authors establish this non-monotonic behavior analytically using Fisher’s Linear Discriminant on synthetic datasets. They also demonstrate it empirically with deep networks on several computer vision benchmarks. The finding concerns the quantity of added data as well as its source: data that is useful in a small amount can become harmful in a larger amount.

When the identity of out-of-distribution samples is known, the authors show that an appropriately weighted training objective can exploit this pattern. They describe this as an idealized setting with limited practical utility. When those identities are unknown, data augmentation, hyperparameter optimization, and pretraining do not ensure protection against deterioration as more such samples are added. The results suggest possible value in detecting and weighting these samples, without guaranteeing that standard training practices will manage them successfully.
icml-2023-the-value-of-out-of-distributi.tldr: Small amounts of out-of-distribution data can improve generalization even when larger amounts make it worse than using none.

paragraphs: Evidential neural networks represent classification uncertainty by turning network outputs into evidence that parameterizes a Dirichlet distribution. The paper identifies a training problem when inherently uncertain examples receive one-hot labels: evidence for mislabeled classes can be penalized too strongly, hindering the learning process.

The proposed Fisher Information-based Evidential Deep Learning method measures how informative each sample’s evidence is using the Fisher Information Matrix. It then dynamically reweights terms in the training objective, directing more attention toward learning representations of uncertain classes. The authors additionally optimize a PAC-Bayesian bound to improve generalization.

Across multiple uncertainty-estimation tasks, the method consistently outperforms traditional evidential-learning approaches in the reported experiments. The gains are especially apparent in few-shot classification, where only a small number of examples are available. The contribution connects the treatment of ambiguous training evidence to the reliability of uncertainty estimates: rather than applying the same balance of penalties to every sample, the objective adapts according to the informativeness of its evidence.
icml-2023-uncertainty-estimation-by-fish.tldr: Fisher-information-based loss reweighting improves evidential uncertainty estimation in reported experiments, particularly for few-shot classification.
